{{Short description|Test for heteroscedasticity}}
In [[econometrics]], the '''Park test''' is a test for [[heteroscedasticity]]. The test is based on the method proposed by Rolla Edward Park for estimating [[linear regression]] parameters in the presence of [[heteroscedastic]] [[errors and residuals in statistics|error terms]].<ref name=Park>{{cite journal |last=Park |first=R. E. |year=1966 |title=Estimation with Heteroscedastic Error Terms |journal=[[Econometrica]] |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=888 |jstor=1910108 }}</ref>

==Background==

In [[regression analysis]], [[heteroscedasticity]] refers to unequal [[variance]]s of the [[errors and residuals in statistics|random error terms]] <math>\epsilon_i</math>, such that

:<math>\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_i)=E(\epsilon_i^2)-E(\epsilon_i)^2=E(\epsilon_i^2)=\sigma_i^2</math>.

It is assumed that <math>\operatorname{E}(\epsilon_i)=0</math>. The above variance varies with <math>i</math>, or the <math>i^{th}</math> trial in an experiment or the <math>i^{th}</math>case or observation in a dataset.  Equivalently, heteroscedasticity refers to unequal conditional variances in the response variables <math>Y_i</math>, such that

:<math>\operatorname{Var}(Y_i|X_i)=\sigma_i^2</math>,

again a value that depends on <math>i</math> – or, more specifically, a value that is conditional on the values of one or more of the regressors <math>X</math>.  [[Homoscedasticity]], one of the basic [[Gauss–Markov theorem|Gauss–Markov]] assumptions of [[ordinary least squares]] [[linear regression]] modeling, refers to equal variance in the random error terms regardless of the trial or observation, such that

:<math>\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_i)=\sigma^2</math>, a constant.

===Test description===

Park, on noting a standard recommendation of assuming proportionality between error term variance and the square of the regressor, suggested instead that analysts 'assume a structure for the variance of the error term' and suggested one such structure:<ref name=Park/>

:<math>\operatorname{ln}(\sigma_{\epsilon i}^2)=\operatorname{ln}(\sigma^2)=\gamma\operatorname{ln}(X_i)+v_i</math>

in which the error terms <math>v_i</math> are considered well behaved.

This relationship is used as the basis for this test.

The modeler first runs the unadjusted regression

:<math>Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+...+\beta_{p-1}X_{i,p-1}+\epsilon_i</math>

where the latter contains ''p''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 regressors, and then squares and takes the natural logarithm of each of the [[errors and residuals in statistics|residuals]] (<math>\hat{\epsilon_i}</math>), which serve as estimators of the <math>\epsilon_i</math>. The squared residuals <math>\hat{\epsilon_i}^2</math> in turn estimate <math>\sigma_{\epsilon i}^2</math>.

If, then, in a regression of <math>\ln{(\epsilon_i^2)}</math> on the natural logarithm of one or more of the regressors <math>X_i</math>, we arrive at statistical significance for non-zero values on one or more of the <math>\hat\gamma_i</math>, we reveal a connection between the residuals and the regressors. We reject the null hypothesis of homoscedasticity and conclude that heteroscedasticity is present.

==Notes==

The test has been discussed in econometrics textbooks.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gujarati |first=Damodar |year=1988 |title=Basic Econometrics |edition=2nd |location=New York |publisher=McGraw–Hill |isbn=0-07-100446-7 |pages=329–330 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=A. H. |last=Studenmund |title=Using Econometrics: A Practical Guide |url=https://archive.org/details/usingeconometric00stud_064 |url-access=limited |edition=Fourth |location=Boston |publisher=Addison-Wesley |year=2001 |isbn=0-321-06481-X |pages=[https://archive.org/details/usingeconometric00stud_064/page/n352 356]–358 }}</ref> [[Stephen Goldfeld]] and [[Richard E. Quandt]] raise concerns about the assumed structure, cautioning that the v<sub>i</sub> may be heteroscedastic and otherwise violate assumptions of ordinary least squares regression.<ref>Goldfeld, Stephen M.; Quandt, Richard E. (1972) ''Nonlinear Methods in Econometrics'', Amsterdam:  North Holland Publishing Company, pp. 93–94. Referred to in: Gujarati, Damodar (1988) ''Basic Econometrics'' (2nd Edition), New York: McGraw-Hill, p. 329.</ref>
